# Review of Last Class

## Indicator Variables and Mixed Integer Programming

Binary decisions need **indicator variables** $u \in \{0, 1\}$:

- changes decision problem to **mixed integer**;
- write **conditional** constraints or objectives using indicators;
- basic solution algorithm is **branch and bound**.

# Solid Waste Management

## Waste Load Allocation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
Some relevant questions:

- Where do we send waste?
- What types of facilities do we build/operate?
:::
::: {.column width=50%}

![Waste Management Hierarchy](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/styles/medium/public/2015-08/hierarchy_hierarchy_and_options_pages.png){width=100%}

::: {.caption}
Source: [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/homeland-security-waste/waste-management-options-homeland-security-incidents)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Waste management options form a hierarchy: reduce first, then recycle, then recover energy, and landfill last. There are a variety of types of facilities, and a waste management plan requires deciding which facilities to build or operate.
:::

## Waste Allocation As A Network

Waste moves as *flows* between waste sources and sinks (disposal sites) based on transportation networks.

![Network Representation](figures/waste-network-blank.svg){width=75%}

::: {.notes}
A network has nodes and edges. We want to decide how to allocate waste given the restrictions of the road network as well as processing any residual waste.
:::

## Network and Decision Parameterization

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
![Network Parameterization](figures/waste-network-params.svg)
:::
::: {.column width=50%}

| Variable | Definition |
| :--: | :------- |
| $\color{purple}S_i$ | Waste produced at source $i$ (Mg/day) |
| $\color{red}K_j$ | Capacity of disposal $j$ (Mg/day) |
| $\color{blue}W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from source $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) |

:::
::::
## Conservation at Each Node

**Mass balance** holds at each facility:

- A waste source does not hold onto any waste, $\sum_j W_{ij} = S_i$,
- Incoming flows at a disposal facility have to balance with waste disposal and outflows of residual waste (*e.g.* material that cannot be recycled).

:::

## Example System

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=60%}
![Waste Management Example](figures/waste-example-network.svg)
:::
::: {.column width=40%}
We do not have to operate all facilities.

The MRF and WTE reduce waste mass but create residuals which must be further disposed of.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Note the edges between facilities: the MRF sends its residual to the WTE or the landfill, and the WTE sends its ash to the landfill.
:::

## Decision Variables

***What are our decision variables?***

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Variable | Definition
:--: | :-----
$W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from city $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day)
$R_{kj}$ | Residual waste transported from disposal $k$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day)
$Y_j$ | Operational status (on/off) of disposal $j$ (binary)
:::

## Objective: Minimize Costs

- **Transportation**: transporting waste has a per-weight cost $a_{ij}$ (\$/Mg-km) times the distance $l_{ij}$ (km).
- **Disposal**: facilities have a fixed cost to operate $c_j$ (\$/day) and a variable tipping cost $b_j$ (\$/Mg).

$$\begin{aligned}
Y_j &= \begin{cases}0 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is not operated} \\ 1 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is operated} \end{cases}\\
\text{Disposal cost} &= \sum_j \left[c_j \, Y_j + b_j \times (\text{everything arriving at } j)\right]
\end{aligned}$$

## Costs For Our Problem

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("| Facility | Fixed cost (\\\$/yr) | Fixed cost (\\\$/day) | Tipping (\\\$/Mg) | Capacity (Mg/day) |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for j in 1:3
    println("| ", ["WTE (1)", "MRF (2)", "LF (3)"][j], " | ", commas(fixed_cost_year[j]), " | ", commas(fixed_cost[j]),
        " | ", tipping[j], " | ", capacity[j], " |")
end
```

Transport costs \$`{julia} @sprintf("%.2f", transport_rate)`/Mg-km. The MRF recycles `{julia} round(Int, 100 * recycle_rate)`% of what it receives, at \$`{julia} recycle_cost`/Mg recycled, and passes on the rest; the WTE leaves `{julia} round(Int, 100 * ash_rate)`% of its input as ash.

::: {.notes}
The daily fixed costs are the annual costs divided by 365. The MRF is cheap to run but the `{julia} round(Int, 100 * (1 - recycle_rate))`% it does not recycle still has to go to the WTE or the landfill.
:::


## Calculating the Objective

The objective adds up each facility's fixed cost, the tipping on what arrives (and, at the MRF, the recycling cost), and the hauling, **e.g. for the MRF**:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

# The MRF's terms in the objective, from the data
gate = tipping[2] + recycle_rate * recycle_cost             # [$/Mg arriving]
in_1, in_2 = city_distance[1, 2], city_distance[2, 2]       # [km] from each city
mrf_terms = (fixed=fixed_cost[2], W12=gate + transport_rate * in_1, W22=gate + transport_rate * in_2,
    R21=transport_rate * mrf_to_wte, R23=transport_rate * mrf_to_lf)
@assert mrf_terms.W12 ≈ city_cost[1, 2] && mrf_terms.W22 ≈ city_cost[2, 2]
println("\$\$")
println("\\begin{aligned}")
println("& \\underbrace{", replace(commas(fixed_cost[2]), "," => "{,}"), "\\,Y_2}_{\\text{fixed cost}}",
    " + \\underbrace{($(tipping[2]) + $(recycle_rate) \\times $(recycle_cost))\\,(W_{12} + W_{22})}_{\\text{tipping and recycling}} \\\\")
println("& + \\underbrace{$(transport_rate)\\,($(in_1)\\,W_{12} + $(in_2)\\,W_{22})}_{\\text{hauling in}}",
    " + \\underbrace{$(transport_rate)\\,($(mrf_to_wte)\\,R_{21} + $(mrf_to_lf)\\,R_{23})}_{\\text{hauling its residual out}} \\\\[0.6em]")
println("& = ", replace(commas(fixed_cost[2]), "," => "{,}"), "\\,Y_2 + ", fmt(mrf_terms.W12), "\\,W_{12} + ",
    fmt(mrf_terms.W22), "\\,W_{22} + ", fmt(mrf_terms.R21), "\\,R_{21} + ", fmt(mrf_terms.R23), "\\,R_{23}")
println("\\end{aligned}")
println("\$\$")
```

## Mass Balance for Sources and Residuals

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=45%}
Outflows from cities have to match produced waste:

$W_{11} + W_{12} + W_{13} =$ `{julia} waste[1]`

$W_{21} + W_{22} + W_{23} =$ `{julia} waste[2]`
:::
::: {.column width=55%}
::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Facilities can produce residual waste (outflows after processing):

WTE ash:
$$R_{13} = 0.2\,(W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21})$$

MRF residual:
$$R_{21} + R_{23} = 0.6\,(W_{12} + W_{22})$$
:::
:::
::::

## Capacity Constraints

Need to modify capacity constraints to ensure that a closed facility receives no waste:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{WTE:}& \quad W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} \leq 150\,Y_1 \\
\text{MRF:}& \quad W_{12} + W_{22} \leq 130\,Y_2 \\
\text{LF:}& \quad W_{13} + W_{23} + R_{13} + R_{23} \leq 200\,Y_3
\end{aligned}
$$


## The Full Problem {.smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

# The example's problem with its coefficients: $/Mg for flows, $/day for the binaries
term(c, v) = fmt(c) * "\\," * v
city_terms = join([term(city_cost[i, j], "W_{$(i)$(j)}") for i in 1:2 for j in 1:3], " + ")
fixed_terms = join([replace(commas(fixed_cost[j]), "," => "{,}") * "\\,Y_$(j)" for j in 1:3], " + ")
println("\$\$")
println("\\begin{aligned}")
println("\\min_{\\mathbf{W}, \\mathbf{R}, \\mathbf{Y}} \\quad & ", city_terms, " \\\\")
println("& + ", term(cost_R21, "R_{21}"), " + ", term(cost_R23, "R_{23}"), " + ", term(cost_R13, "R_{13}"),
    " + ", fixed_terms, " \\\\[0.4em]")
println("\\text{subject to:} \\quad & W_{11} + W_{12} + W_{13} = $(waste[1]) \\qquad \\text{(City 1)} \\\\")
println("& W_{21} + W_{22} + W_{23} = $(waste[2]) \\qquad \\text{(City 2)} \\\\")
println("& R_{13} = $(ash_rate)\\,(W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21}) \\qquad \\text{(WTE ash)} \\\\")
println("& R_{21} + R_{23} = $(1 - recycle_rate)\\,(W_{12} + W_{22}) \\qquad \\text{(MRF residual)} \\\\")
println("& W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} \\leq $(capacity[1])\\,Y_1 \\qquad \\text{(WTE capacity)} \\\\")
println("& W_{12} + W_{22} \\leq $(capacity[2])\\,Y_2 \\qquad \\text{(MRF capacity)} \\\\")
println("& W_{13} + W_{23} + R_{13} + R_{23} \\leq $(capacity[3])\\,Y_3 \\qquad \\text{(LF capacity)} \\\\")
println("& W_{ij},\\, R_{kj} \\geq 0, \\quad Y_j \\in \\{0, 1\\}")
println("\\end{aligned}")
println("\$\$")
```

## Writing the Model in JuMP

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output: false

# The model as formulated on the previous slides
function waste_model(; landfill_capacity=capacity[3])
    cap = [capacity[1], capacity[2], landfill_capacity]
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    @variable(model, W[1:2, 1:3] >= 0)   # city i -> facility j [Mg/day]
    @variable(model, R21 >= 0)           # MRF residual -> WTE
    @variable(model, R23 >= 0)           # MRF residual -> LF
    @variable(model, R13 >= 0)           # WTE ash -> LF
    @variable(model, Y[1:3], Bin)        # facility operates?
    @objective(model, Min,
        sum(city_cost[i, j] * W[i, j] for i in 1:2, j in 1:3) +
        cost_R21 * R21 + cost_R23 * R23 + cost_R13 * R13 +
        sum(fixed_cost[j] * Y[j] for j in 1:3))
    @constraint(model, city[i in 1:2], sum(W[i, :]) == waste[i])
    @constraint(model, ash, R13 == ash_rate * (W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21))
    @constraint(model, residual,
        R21 + R23 == (1 - recycle_rate) * (W[1, 2] + W[2, 2]))
    @constraint(model, wte, W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21 <= cap[1] * Y[1])
    @constraint(model, mrf, W[1, 2] + W[2, 2] <= cap[2] * Y[2])
    @constraint(model, lf, W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23 <= cap[3] * Y[3])
    return model
end
```

::: {.notes}
You also don't need to walk through this: they've seen the relevant parts of setting up a MILP.
:::

## Solving the Example in JuMP

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: asis

# The optimal flows, on/off decisions and cost of a solved model
function solution(model)
    W, Y = model[:W], model[:Y]
    R21, R23, R13 = model[:R21], model[:R23], model[:R13]
    return (cost=objective_value(model), Y=round.(Int, value.(Y)),
        W=value.(W), R21=value(R21), R23=value(R23), R13=value(R13),
        lf_load=value(W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23))
end

base_model = waste_model()
optimize!(base_model)
base = solution(base_model)

# The solution as a table
println("| Solution | Value |")
println("|:--|--:|")
println("| Cost (\\\$/day) | ", commas(base.cost), " |")
println("| \$Y\$ (WTE, MRF, LF) | ", join(base.Y, ", "), " |")
println("| \$W_{1j}\$, City 1 to WTE, MRF, LF (Mg/day) | ", join(fmt.(base.W[1, :]), ", "), " |")
println("| \$W_{2j}\$, City 2 to WTE, MRF, LF (Mg/day) | ", join(fmt.(base.W[2, :]), ", "), " |")
println("| \$R_{21}\$, \$R_{23}\$, \$R_{13}\$ (Mg/day) | ", join(fmt.([base.R21, base.R23, base.R13]), ", "), " |")
```

::: {.notes}
Most important: Y line, where all facilities are operated. Then City 1 sends everything to the MRF, City 2 sends everything to the LF.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=55%}
![Waste Management Problem Solution](figures/waste-example-solution.svg)
:::
::: {.column width=45%}
| Flow | Mg/day |
|:--|--:|
| City 1 → MRF | `{julia} fmt(base.W[1, 2])` |
| City 2 → LF | `{julia} fmt(base.W[2, 3])` |
| MRF residual → WTE | `{julia} fmt(base.R21)` |
| MRF residual → LF | `{julia} fmt(base.R23)` |
| WTE ash → LF | `{julia} fmt(base.R13)` |
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The MRF's residual is split between the WTE and the landfill.
:::

## Shadow Prices for a MILP

- Shadow prices are not well-defined for MILPs as they are for LPs because an indicator variable can only switch between 0 and 1.
- One approach: Fix the indicators at their optimal values to produce an LP with the same solution.
- This LP's shadow prices are **conditional** on that choice: they describe small changes with the same facilities running.

::: {.notes}
If a change is large enough that the cheapest plan opens or closes a facility, the conditional shadow price no longer describes the change in the objective (just like sufficiently large changes for LPs), because the change in fixed costs creates a discontinuity.
:::

## MIP Shadow Prices in `JuMP`

```julia
optimize!(model)                  # the MILP: no shadow prices yet
fix_discrete_variables(model)     # fix each Y_j at its optimal 0 or 1
optimize!(model)                  # an LP with the same solution
shadow_price(lf)                  # conditional on which facilities run
```
- By default, `JuMP` reports no shadow prices for a MILP.
- `fix_discrete_variables()` fixes the indicator variables at the optimal values so the rest of the problem becomes an LP.


## Conditional Shadow Prices

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: asis

# Fix the binaries at their optimal values and re-solve: an LP with the same solution
fix_discrete_variables(base_model)
optimize!(base_model)
# Sizes of the shadow prices: for a city, the cost of one more Mg/day of waste;
# for a facility, the saving from one more Mg/day of capacity
base_price = (city=-shadow_price.(base_model[:city]), wte=-shadow_price(base_model[:wte]),
    mrf=-shadow_price(base_model[:mrf]), lf=-shadow_price(base_model[:lf]))
# Landfill space freed per Mg moved from the landfill to the WTE: its ash comes back [Mg]
space_per_Mg = 1 - ash_rate

# The table's sign: + if one more Mg/day raises the cost, - if it lowers it
signed(x) = x > 0.005 ? "+" * money(x) : (x < -0.005 ? "−" * money(-x) : "0.00")
println("| One more Mg/day of | Change in cost (\\\$/day) |")
println("|:--|--:|")
println("| City 1's waste | ", signed(base_price.city[1]), " |")
println("| City 2's waste | ", signed(base_price.city[2]), " |")
println("| WTE capacity | ", signed(-base_price.wte), " |")
println("| MRF capacity | ", signed(-base_price.mrf), " |")
println("| Landfill capacity | ", signed(-base_price.lf), " |")
```

:::
::: {.column width=10%}
:::
::: {.column width=40%}
Moving 1 Mg to the WTE frees only `{julia} space_per_Mg` Mg in the landfill.

So each additional Mg/day of landfill capacity takes `{julia} 1 / space_per_Mg` Mg/day of MRF residual away from the WTE, saving \$`{julia} money(base_price.lf)`/day.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The landfill's capacity is the binding constraint. Every route for new waste has to account for the full landfill.


:::


## What If the Landfill Were Expanded?

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: asis

bigger_capacity = 220
bigger_model = waste_model(landfill_capacity=bigger_capacity)
optimize!(bigger_model)
bigger = solution(bigger_model)
println("| Landfill capacity (Mg/day) | Cost (\\\$/day) | WTE | MRF | LF |")
println("|:--|--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|")
for (lf_capacity, r) in ((capacity[3], base), (bigger_capacity, bigger))
    status = fill("open", 3)
    for j in 1:3
        if r.Y[j] == 0
            status[j] = "**closed**"
        end
    end
    println("| ", lf_capacity, " | ", commas(r.cost), " | ", join(status, " | "), " |")
end
```
With `{julia} bigger_capacity - capacity[3]` Mg/day more landfill capacity, the **WTE closes** and the system saves \$`{julia} commas(base.cost - bigger.cost)`/day.

The landfill's shadow price predicted a saving of only `{julia} bigger_capacity - capacity[3]` × \$`{julia} money(base_price.lf)` = \$`{julia} commas((bigger_capacity - capacity[3]) * base_price.lf)`/day.

::: {.notes}
The shadow price assumes the same facilities run and the same constraints are binding. Here the change is large enough that the WTE closes, and its fixed cost of \$`{julia} commas(fixed_cost[1])`/day goes away, so the actual saving is far larger than the shadow price predicts.
:::

# Limits on Trucking

## City 2's Trucks

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

# City 2's trucks. Each load: a round trip plus unloading
truck_load = 10                                 # [Mg] per truckload
truck_speed = 40                                # [km/h] average
unload_time = 0.25                              # [h] at the facility
hours_per_load = zeros(3)                       # [h] City 2 to facility j and back
for j in 1:3
    hours_per_load[j] = 2 * city_distance[2, j] / truck_speed + unload_time
end
hours_per_Mg = hours_per_load ./ truck_load     # [truck-hours per Mg]
fleet_limit = 24                                # [truck-hours/day] City 2 has for these trips
base_truck_hours = sum(hours_per_Mg .* base.W[2, :])   # the plan so far
```

Suppose City 2's collection trucks also haul its waste to the facilities. We assume each carries `{julia} truck_load` Mg, averages `{julia} truck_speed` km/h and takes `{julia} round(Int, 60 * unload_time)` minutes to unload, so a load takes:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("| From City 2 to | Hours per load | Truck-hours per Mg |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
for j in 1:3
    println("| ", ["WTE", "MRF", "LF"][j], " (", city_distance[2, j], " km) | ", @sprintf("%.2f", hours_per_load[j]),
        " | ", @sprintf("%.3f", hours_per_Mg[j]), " |")
end
```

::: {.notes}
A fleet's time is what usually limits how much a city can haul directly: collection trucks have to collect as well as haul, and a long trip to a distant site takes a truck off its route for longer. (Truck size, speed and unloading time are assumptions for this example; rear-loading collection trucks typically carry about 6 to 19 tons, depending on the body and how tightly the waste is compacted.) The landfill is the farthest facility from City 2, so each Mg sent there takes twice the truck time of a Mg sent to the WTE.

Each load is a round trip plus unloading.
:::

## Limits on City 2's Trucking Capacity

Sending all `{julia} waste[2]` Mg/day to the landfill takes `{julia} fmt(base_truck_hours)` truck-hours a day. Suppose City 2's trucks have only `{julia} fleet_limit` hours.

This produces a new constraint:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("\$\$", @sprintf("%.3f", hours_per_Mg[1]), "\\,W_{21} + ", @sprintf("%.3f", hours_per_Mg[2]),
    "\\,W_{22} + ", @sprintf("%.3f", hours_per_Mg[3]), "\\,W_{23} \\leq ", fleet_limit,
    " \\quad \\text{(truck-hours/day)}\$\$")
```

::: {.notes}
This is an example of a **flow constraint**: it limits outflows along City 2's edges, each weighted by how long the trip takes.
:::

## Re-Solving With the Truck Limit {.smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: asis

# The model as formulated, plus a limit on City 2's truck-hours [truck-hours/day]
function solve_with_truck_limit(fleet_hours)
    model = waste_model()
    W = model[:W]
    @constraint(model, fleet, sum(hours_per_Mg[j] * W[2, j] for j in 1:3) <= fleet_hours)
    optimize!(model)
    result = solution(model)
    truck_hours = sum(hours_per_Mg[j] * result.W[2, j] for j in 1:3)
    fix_discrete_variables(model)               # for the shadow price, as before
    optimize!(model)
    return merge(result, (truck_hours=truck_hours, fleet_price=-shadow_price(fleet)))
end

trucks = solve_with_truck_limit(fleet_limit)
println("| | No limit | $(fleet_limit) truck-hours |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
println("| City 2 → WTE (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.W[2, 1]), " | ", fmt(trucks.W[2, 1]), " |")
println("| City 2 → LF (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.W[2, 3]), " | ", fmt(trucks.W[2, 3]), " |")
println("| MRF residual → WTE (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.R21), " | ", fmt(trucks.R21), " |")
println("| MRF residual → LF (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.R23), " | ", fmt(trucks.R23), " |")
println("| City 2 truck-hours/day | ", fmt(base_truck_hours), " | ", fmt(trucks.truck_hours), " |")
println("| Cost (\\\$/day) | ", commas(base.cost), " | ", commas(trucks.cost), " |")
```

::: {.notes}
The whole network now adjusts to the new constraint. City 2 can cut its truck time only by sending waste somewhere closer than the landfill, and the WTE is the closest. The WTE has room for City 2's waste only if it burns less of the MRF's residual, and that residual then goes to the landfill, which is still operating at full capacity.
:::

## What Is a Truck-Hour Worth?

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

few_hours = 20
few = solve_with_truck_limit(few_hours)
# The truck limit at which the WTE has no MRF residual left to give up [truck-hours/day]
no_residual_hours = base_truck_hours - (hours_per_Mg[3] - hours_per_Mg[1]) * base.R21

# The slides' claims about the truck limit
@assert trucks.truck_hours > fleet_limit - 1e-6                 # the limit binds
@assert all(trucks.Y .== 1) && trucks.R21 > 0
@assert abs(trucks.lf_load - capacity[3]) < 1e-6
@assert trucks.fleet_price > 0
@assert fleet_limit > no_residual_hours
@assert few.Y[2] == 0 && abs(few.fleet_price) < 1e-6
```

The truck limit's shadow price is **\$`{julia} money(trucks.fleet_price)`/day per truck-hour**. One more truck-hour lets City 2 send `{julia} fmt(1 / (hours_per_Mg[3] - hours_per_Mg[1]))` Mg/day to the landfill instead of the WTE, saving \$`{julia} money(trucks.fleet_price * (hours_per_Mg[3] - hours_per_Mg[1]))` per Mg.


# Key Takeaways

## Key Takeaways

- A network model's decisions are **flows** on edges, constrained by **conservation** at each node.
- Waste facilities can produce residuals which need to be processed or disposed of at the next level of the waste disposal hierarchy.
- A **flow constraint** limits edges, not nodes, unlike mass-balance constraints.

## Network Models Elsewhere

- Can have more advanced network models with highly-specified routes:
  - Transportation networks
  - Power transmission networks
  - Pipeline networks
- Flows could also be bidirectional.
